title: Two-Handed Backhand Fundamentals
text: # Two-Handed Backhand Fundamentals ## Overview The two-handed backhand is one of the most reliable groundstrokes in modern tennis. It provides stability, power, and disguise. ## Key Phases ### 1. Preparation - Unit turn: shoulders rotate together - Early racket preparation - Split step before opponent's contact - Weight on back foot ### 2. Load Phase - Hip and shoulder coil - Racket drops below ball level - Knees bent for power generation - Core engagement ### 3. Contact - Hip rotation drives the stroke - Contact point slightly in front - Both hands firm on racket - Eyes on ball through contact ### 4. Follow-Through - Full extension toward target - Racket finishes high (over opposite shoulder) - Weight transfers to front foot - Recovery step back to ready position ## Common Issues **Elbow Angle**: Should be ~150-160° at contact for optimal power transfer. **Hip Rotation**: Minimum 40-45° rotation for power generation. Limited rotation = weak shot. **Stance Width**: 2-2.5 feet for stability. Too narrow = balance issues. ## Pro Tips - Practice shadow swings focusing on hip rotation - Film from the side to check contact point - Use targets to improve consistency before adding power

title: Balance Drift: Stability During Strokes
text: # Balance Drift: Stability During Strokes ## Common Question Phrasing This section covers: What causes balance drift? Why am I losing balance during strokes? What is lateral movement or COM drift? How do I stop swaying sideways? Why am I leaning sideways when hitting? What causes center of mass drift? ## What Is Balance Drift? Balance drift measures lateral (side-to-side) movement of your center of mass (COM) during the stroke. Excessive drift, also called sway or leaning sideways, indicates instability and reduces power transfer. When you lose balance during the stroke, your body drifts laterally instead of staying grounded. ## Why Stability Matters ### Power Transfer - Stable base → efficient energy transfer to ball - Drifting base → energy lost in lateral movement - Result: Drift = weaker, less consistent shots ### Consistency - Stable contact point → predictable ball flight - Drifting contact → variable outcomes - Result: Drift = inconsistency ### Recovery Speed - Stable finish → quick recovery - Drifting finish → extra time to regain balance - Result: Drift = slower court coverage ## Measuring Balance Drift Coach AI tracks your center of mass movement: - **Minimal drift**: <5cm lateral movement - **Moderate drift**: 5-10cm - **Excessive drift**: >10cm Stability score (0-100): Higher = more stable ## Common Causes of Balance Drift Quick summary - Balance drift happens when: - **Stance too narrow** (feet too close = unstable base) - **Poor weight transfer** (losing balance, momentum carries you sideways) - **Weak core** (torso sways, can't stabilize) - **Overreaching** (stretching too far, leaning sideways) - **Fatigue** (tired muscles can't maintain stability) ### Detailed Causes ### 1. Stance Too Narrow **Problem**: Feet too close together **Result**: Unstable base, easy to knock off balance, causes lateral drift **Fix**: Widen stance to 2-2.5 feet ### 2. Poor Weight Transfer **Problem**: Excessive weight shift without control **Result**: Momentum carries you off balance, swaying sideways **Fix**: Controlled weight transfer, front foot plants firmly ### 3. Weak Core **Problem**: Core can't stabilize trunk **Result**: Torso sways during stroke, center of mass drifts **Fix**: Core strengthening exercises ### 4. Overreaching **Problem**: Stretching too far for ball **Result**: Off-balance contact, leaning sideways **Fix**: Better court positioning, earlier preparation ### 5. Fatigue **Problem**: Tired stabilizer muscles **Result**: Progressive drift increases through session **Fix**: Conditioning + manage training load ## How to Fix Balance Drift **Immediate fixes:** - Widen your stance (2-2.5 feet) - Engage core before every stroke - Plant front foot firmly during contact - Stop overreaching for balls **Training fixes:** - Core strengthening (planks, side planks, rotational exercises) - Balance drills (single-leg exercises, wobble board) - Proper footwork patterns - Video analysis to see your drift patterns ## Technical Corrections ### Stance Width - **Check**: Feet 2-2.5 feet apart at contact - **Feel**: Stable, grounded, athletic position - **Drill**: Shadow swings with exaggerated wide stance ### Weight Distribution - **Check**: 60% front foot, 40% back foot at contact - **Feel**: Balanced, not falling forward/backward - **Drill**: Contact position holds (freeze at contact for

**Check**: Abs tight, trunk stable - **Feel**: Solid, connected feeling - **Drill**: Planks, side planks, rotational exercises ### Head Position - **Check**: Head level, not bobbing - **Feel**: Eyes level with horizon - **Drill**: Balance beam practice, eyes closed shadow swings ## Physical Training ### Strengthening - **Core**: Planks, bird dogs, dead bugs - **Legs**: Squats, lunges (especially lateral lunges) - **Ankles**: Single-leg balance, wobble board ### Balance Training - **Static**: Single-leg stands, eyes closed balance - **Dynamic**: Balance board strokes, unstable surface practice - **Reactive**: Reaction ball catches while on one leg ### Proprioception - **Eyes closed drills**: Shadow swings without visual feedback - **Unstable surfaces**: BOSU ball, balance board - **Perturbation training**: Partner gently pushes during shadow swings ## Session Patterns ### Early Session (Fresh) - Minimal drift expected - Good stability and control - Baseline measurement ### Mid Session - Slight drift increase acceptable - Maintain stability focus - Monitor for excessive change ### Late Session (Fatigued) - Drift typically increases 20-40% - If >40% increase → fatigue is high - Consider ending session or reducing intensity ## Drift vs Technique ### Technique-Driven Drift - Present from first stroke - Consistent pattern (always same direction/magnitude) - Improves with focus and awareness - Correctable through technical adjustment ### Fatigue-Driven Drift - Increases progressively during session - Variable pattern (random directions) - Doesn't improve with focus when tired - Requires rest/recovery ## Integration with Coach AI When Coach AI flags balance drift: 1. **Check technique first**: Stance width, weight transfer, core engagement 2. **Assess fatigue**: Is it worse late in session? 3. **Review trends**: Getting better or worse over sessions? 4. **Adjust training**: More balance work or more recovery ## Realistic Expectations Perfect stability is rare. Acceptable targets: - **Elite**: <3cm drift, stability score >85 - **Advanced**: <5cm drift, stability score >75 - **Intermediate**: <8cm drift, stability score >65 - **Development**: <10cm drift, stability score >55 Progress gradually. Even 10-20% improvement is significant. ## Drills Specifically for Balance 1. **Single-leg shadow swings**: Execute backhand on one leg 2. **Balance board strokes**: Shadow swings on unstable surface 3. **Freeze drills**: Hold contact position for 5 seconds, check stability 4. **Eyes closed practice**: Remove visual feedback to enhance proprioception 5. **Perturbation drills**: Partner pushes gently during stroke, resist drift Consistent practice builds the neuromuscular patterns for automatic stability.

title: Drill Explanations: How and Why
text: # Drill Explanations: How and Why ## Understanding Drill Purpose Drills are prescribed to address specific technical or physical deficiencies. Understanding the "why" helps you focus correctly during execution. ## Common Drill Categories ### 1. Wall Drills (Hip Rotation) **Purpose**: Improve hip rotation and core engagement **How to Execute**: - Stand with back against wall - Feet shoulder-width apart, 6 inches from wall - Execute backhand motion - Goal: Maintain back contact while rotating hips 40-45° **Why It Works**: - Prevents over-rotation (staying grounded) - Forces core-driven rotation (not arm swing) - Builds kinesthetic awareness of proper hip turn **Key Focus**: Feel the core muscles engage, not just arms swinging --- ### 2. Mirror Shadow Swings **Purpose**: Refine technique fundamentals without ball **How to Execute**: - Stand in front of mirror - Execute slow-motion strokes (50% speed) - Focus on one element (e.g., elbow angle, hip turn) - 3 sets of 10 perfect repetitions **Why It Works**: - Visual feedback reinforces correct patterns - Slow motion builds neuromuscular control - No ball = 100% focus on technique **Key Focus**: Quality over quantity; perfection at slow speed first --- ### 3. Cross-Court Rallies (Consistency) **Purpose**: Build stroke reliability and rhythm **How to Execute**: - Rally cross-court only - Goal: 20+ consecutive shots - Moderate pace (70% effort) - Focus on contact point and follow-through **Why It Works**: - Cross-court is highest percentage shot - Rhythm develops timing and feel - Consistency before power **Key Focus**: Same contact point every time --- ### 4. Cone Footwork Drills **Purpose**: Improve lateral movement and recovery **How to Execute**: - Place cones 10-15 feet apart - Side shuffle between cones - Touch cone, split step, change direction - 3 sets of 30 seconds **Why It Works**: - Builds explosive lateral push-off - Trains split step timing - Conditions legs for match play **Key Focus**: First step explosion, low center of mass --- ### 5. Balance Board Strokes **Purpose**: Improve balance and stability during stroke **How to Execute**: - Stand on balance board or unstable surface - Execute slow shadow swings - Maintain balance throughout stroke - 2 sets of 10 strokes **Why It Works**: - Strengthens stabilizer muscles - Forces core engagement - Improves proprioception **Key Focus**: Smooth, controlled movement --- ## Drill Intensity Guidelines ### Intensive (CRITICAL Issues) - Daily practice - High volume (30+ minutes) - May include resistance (bands, weighted racket) - Rest 1 day per week ### Moderate (PRIORITY Issues) - 3-5x per week - Standard volume (15-20 minutes) - Focus on perfect execution - Mix with match play ### Light (MONITOR/Maintain) - 2-3x per week - Lower volume (10 minutes) - Maintain progress, not build new skills - Can be warm-up component ## Progression Principles 1. **Master basics before advancing**: Perfect slow before fast 2. **Consistency before complexity**: Reliable execution, then variations 3. **Technique before power**: Form first, then increase intensity 4. **Isolate then integrate**: Drill specific, then apply in play ## Drill Effectiveness Coach AI tracks which drills improve

title: Fatigue vs Technique Issues
text: # Fatigue vs Technique Issues ## The Challenge When performance drops, is it fatigue or technique regression? Understanding the difference guides your training decisions. ## Fatigue Signals ### Biomechanical Indicators - **Recovery time increases**: Taking longer to return to ready position - **Range of motion decreases**: Hip rotation, shoulder turn become limited - **Variability increases**: Inconsistent stroke patterns - **Balance instability**: More lateral drift, unsteady stance - **Movement quality declines**: Slower footwork, less explosive ### Pattern Recognition Fatigue typically affects: 1. Lower body first (legs, footwork) 2. Core stability 3. Fine motor control last (touch, feel) ## Technique Issues ### Biomechanical Indicators - **Consistent errors**: Same mistake repeatedly - **Phase-specific problems**: Issue isolated to one movement phase - **Present when fresh**: Error occurs even at session start - **Compensations visible**: Body adjusts incorrectly to execute stroke ### Pattern Recognition Technique issues: 1. Appear regardless of fatigue level 2. Often phase-specific (e.g., poor preparation only) 3. Can be corrected with focus/awareness 4. May worsen under fatigue but root cause is technical ## How to Differentiate ### Ask These Questions 1. **Does the issue improve with rest?** → Fatigue 2. **Is it present from the first stroke?** → Technique 3. **Does it worsen progressively during session?** → Fatigue 4. **Is it consistent across multiple sessions?** → Technique 5. **Does conscious focus improve it immediately?** → Technique ### Mixed Cases Often it's both: - Fatigue exposes technique weaknesses - Poor technique accelerates fatigue - Address both for optimal improvement ## Training Implications ### If Fatigue-Driven - Prioritize recovery - Reduce training volume - Focus on conditioning - Monitor readiness before sessions ### If Technique-Driven - Increase deliberate practice - Slow-motion repetition - Video analysis - Drill-based correction ### If Mixed - Address technique when fresh - Build conditioning to maintain technique under fatigue - Progressive overload: technique → volume → intensity ## Coach AI Context Coach AI detects fatigue through: - Recovery time trends - Movement quality degradation - Metric variability increases - Session-to-session patterns Use this alongside your self-awareness and coach feedback.

title: How to Film for Best Analysis
text: # How to Film for Best Analysis ## Camera Setup ### Position - **Side view (most important)**: 90° perpendicular to baseline - **Distance**: 15-20 feet away - **Height**: Waist to chest height - **Stability**: Use tripod or stable surface (not handheld) ### Frame Composition - Full body visible throughout stroke - Some space above head and below feet - Enough width to capture full follow-through - Consistent framing (don't zoom/pan during stroke) ## Lighting ### Best Conditions - Outdoor: Overcast day (even lighting) - Indoor: Bright, even court lighting - Avoid: Backlighting (sun behind player) - Avoid: Strong shadows that obscure body parts ### Problem Solving - If one side of body is shadowed, move camera angle - If background is too bright, adjust camera exposure - Multiple light sources better than single harsh light ## Video Quality ### Settings - **Resolution**: 1080p minimum (4K better for detail) - **Frame rate**: 30fps minimum, 60fps ideal for slow motion - **Focus**: Lock focus on player (disable autofocus if possible) - **Codec**: H.264 recommended for compatibility ### File Management - Short clips (5-15 seconds) easier to analyze than long videos - Multiple strokes from same angle = consistent data - Name files descriptively: date_stroke_view.mp4 ## What to Capture ### Stroke Types - Backhand: Side view is primary - Forehand: Side view + optional front view - Serve: Side and front views both valuable ### Number of Strokes - Minimum: 3-5 strokes per session - Ideal: 10-15 strokes for consistency analysis - Include: Some easy rallies + some under pressure ## Common Mistakes to Avoid 1. **Too Close**: Can't see full body movement 2. **Handheld**: Shaky footage confuses pose detection 3. **Moving Camera**: Tracking player breaks analysis 4. **Cluttered Background**: Busy backgrounds reduce landmark accuracy 5. **Inconsistent Angles**: Can't compare sessions reliably ## Analysis Tips ### Before Filming - Warm up thoroughly (cold technique isn't representative) - Use consistent ball feed (toss, drop feed, or rally) - Mark camera position for session-to-session consistency ### During Filming - Focus on natural strokes (not exaggerated technique) - Mix practice strokes with competitive intensity - Film at different fatigue levels if studying endurance ### After Filming - Review footage before leaving court - Check: full body visible, stable frame, good lighting - Re-film if quality issues detected ## MediaPipe Requirements ### What the AI Needs to See - Clear view of all body landmarks - Shoulders, elbows, wrists, hips, knees, ankles - No occlusion (don't turn away from camera mid-stroke) - Contrasting clothing (solid colors better than patterns) ### Best Practices - Wear fitted clothing (loose clothes obscure body position) - Contrasting color to background - Good lighting on all body parts - Clean, uncluttered background ## Session Consistency For best progress tracking: - Use same camera position each session - Same distance and height - Same court location - Same lighting conditions (time of day) This allows session-to-session comparison and baseline analysis.

title: Footwork & Movement Fundamentals
text: # Footwork & Movement Fundamentals ## Common Question Phrasing This section covers: How do I improve my footwork? What is a split step? When should I split step? How do I move better on court? What is split-step timing? How do I fix my split step? What is good footwork in tennis? ## Why Footwork Matters Good footwork puts you in position to execute technique. Poor footwork forces compensations that lead to errors. ## Split Step ### What It Is A small hop performed as your opponent contacts the ball. It loads your legs like springs for explosive movement. ### Timing - Execute split step DURING opponent's forward swing - Land as they make contact - Feet shoulder-width apart - Weight on balls of feet ### Common Errors - Too early: Lands before opponent's contact → lose momentum - Too late: After contact → slow reaction - Too high: Wastes energy, slow recovery ## Recovery Time ### Definition Time from your contact to return-to-ready position. Elite players: <1.5 seconds. ### Components 1. Deceleration after stroke 2. Change of direction 3. Return to center or tactical position 4. Split step preparation ### Improving Recovery - Push off with outside leg (not hop) - Keep center of mass low - Use small adjustment steps, not big strides - Anticipate based on your shot placement ## Lateral Movement ### Push-Off Technique - Load outside leg - Drive laterally with explosive push - First step is long, subsequent steps shorter - Stay low through the movement ### Balance Maintain balance by: - Wide base during stroke - Core engagement - Controlled deceleration - Eyes level (no head bobbing) ## Drills - Side-to-side shuffle with split step - Shadow swings with recovery step - Cone drills for lateral speed - Balance board for stability training

title: Forehand Fundamentals
text: # Forehand Fundamentals ## Overview The forehand is typically a player's strongest weapon. Modern forehands emphasize rotation, lag, and racket head speed. ## Key Phases ### 1. Preparation - Unit turn with shoulders - Early racket take-back - Non-dominant hand guides racket - Split step before opponent's contact - Weight shifts to back foot ### 2. Load Phase - Hip and shoulder coil (separation) - Racket drops below ball level ("lag") - Knees bend for power - Core winds up like a spring ### 3. Contact - Hip rotation initiates (not arm swing) - Contact point well in front of body - Wrist firm at contact - Eyes on ball - Weight transfers forward ### 4. Follow-Through - Racket wraps around body - Full extension across body - Deceleration over opposite shoulder - Weight fully transferred to front foot - Recovery step begins ## Key Metrics ### Hip Rotation - **Target**: 60-80° rotation from load to follow-through - **Why**: Hip rotation generates 60% of power - **Common issue**: Arm-dominant swing with limited hip rotation ### Elbow Angle at Contact - **Target**: 140-160° (semi-extended) - **Why**: Allows power transfer + control - **Common issue**: Too bent (weak) or too straight (loss of control) ### Wrist Angle - **Target**: Stable through contact, then release - **Why**: Firm wrist at contact = consistent strike - **Common issue**: Early wrist break = loss of power and control ### Stance - **Open stance**: Modern style, good for high balls and time pressure - **Semi-open**: Balance of power and recovery - **Closed stance**: Best for low balls and running forehands - **Width**: 2.5-3 feet for stability ## Common Errors ### 1. Arm-Dominant Swing - **Symptom**: Limited hip rotation, arm does all the work - **Result**: Inconsistent power, prone to injury - **Fix**: Wall drill focusing on hip turn, arm follows ### 2. Late Preparation - **Symptom**: Rushed take-back, short backswing - **Result**: Weak shot, poor timing - **Fix**: Earlier unit turn, shadow swings with metronome ### 3. Inconsistent Contact Point - **Symptom**: Sometimes early, sometimes late - **Result**: Erratic ball flight - **Fix**: Feed drills, focus on contact point only ### 4. Poor Balance - **Symptom**: Falling forward/backward during stroke - **Result**: Inconsistency, slow recovery - **Fix**: Balance drills, wider stance, core strengthening ## Forehand vs Backhand Key differences: - **Forehand**: More hip rotation (60-80° vs 40-45°) - **Forehand**: More arm extension at contact - **Forehand**: Typically more power potential - **Backhand**: Two hands provide more stability - **Backhand**: Less rotation needed, easier consistency Don't expect identical metrics between strokes. ## Grip Considerations ### Eastern Forehand - Traditional, versatile - Good for all ball heights - Easier to transition to volleys ### Semi-Western - Modern standard - Excellent for high balls - Natural topspin generation ### Western - Extreme topspin - Great for clay courts - Struggles with low balls Coach AI analyzes your biomechanics regardless of grip, but grip affects optimal ranges. ## Training Progression 1. **Fundamentals**: Consistent contact, basic rotation 2. **Power**: Increase hip

title: Match Readiness: Understanding Your Competitive State
text: # Match Readiness: Understanding Your Competitive State ## What Is Match Readiness? Match readiness is a synthesis score (0-100) that combines: - **Technique quality**: Your stroke biomechanics - **Movement quality**: Footwork, balance, recovery - **Fatigue level**: Physical freshness - **Signal trust**: Measurement confidence It answers: "How prepared am I to compete today?" ## Readiness Levels ### Excellent (80-100) - **Technical**: All strokes executing well - **Movement**: Quick, balanced, explosive - **Fatigue**: Fresh, no degradation signs - **Recommendation**: Full training or competition ready ### Good (65-79) - **Technical**: Solid with minor issues - **Movement**: Functional with room for improvement - **Fatigue**: Mild signs, manageable - **Recommendation**: Normal training, competition viable ### Fair (50-64) - **Technical**: Noticeable issues present - **Movement**: Some limitations - **Fatigue**: Moderate, affecting performance - **Recommendation**: Technique focus, light competition ### Poor (<50) - **Technical**: Multiple significant issues - **Movement**: Compromised - **Fatigue**: High, performance impacted - **Recommendation**: Recovery or light technique work only ## What Readiness Is NOT ### It's Not Performance Prediction - Doesn't predict match outcome - Doesn't account for opponent skill - Doesn't consider mental state or tactics ### It's Not Medical Diagnosis - Not injury assessment - Not health screening - Not clearance to play ### It's Not Permanent - Changes session to session - Affected by training, recovery, technique work - Can improve or decline based on your actions ## Using Readiness for Decisions ### Competition Timing - **Excellent/Good**: Compete with confidence - **Fair**: Competition possible but expect challenges - **Poor**: Consider postponing if possible ### Training Planning - **Excellent**: Opportunity for intense training - **Good**: Normal progression - **Fair**: Focus on weaknesses, moderate intensity - **Poor**: Recovery priority ### Confidence Building - Track readiness trends - Compete when readiness is rising - Build confidence through preparation ## Contributors Explained ### Technique (35% weight) Based on stroke biomechanics: - Hip rotation, elbow angle, wrist position - Phase-by-phase execution - Consistency across strokes **Interpretation**: - High technique score → Strokes are sound - Low technique score → Technical work needed ### Movement (30% weight) Based on footwork metrics: - Split step timing and quality - Recovery time - Balance and stability **Interpretation**: - High movement score → Court coverage excellent - Low movement score → Footwork/conditioning needed ### Fatigue (20% weight) Based on degradation signals: - Recovery time increases - Balance instability - Metric variability **Interpretation**: - Low fatigue → Fresh, sustainable performance - High fatigue → Need recovery or load reduction ### Signal Trust (15% weight) Based on measurement quality: - Landmark visibility - Tracking stability - Data completeness **Interpretation**: - High trust → Reliable measurements - Low trust → Re-record with better setup ## Confidence Score Every readiness calculation includes a confidence score: - **High confidence (>80%)**: All components present, reliable - **Medium confidence (60-80%)**: Some components missing or uncertain - **Low confidence (<60%)**: Limited data, take with caution Always consider confidence when interpreting readiness. ## Session-to-Session Patterns ### Improving Trend - Readiness scores increasing - **Action**: Continue current training approach

Combine it with self-awareness and professional guidance. ## Key Takeaway Match readiness is a training guidance signal, not a verdict. Use it to: - Optimize training timing - Plan competitions strategically - Detect overtraining early - Build confidence through preparation Combined with your experience and coaching, it helps you make better decisions.

title: Recovery Time: What It Means and Why It Matters
text: # Recovery Time: What It Means and Why It Matters ## Common Question Phrasing This section covers: Why is my recovery time important? What is recovery time? How do I reduce recovery time? Why am I slow getting back to ready position? What causes slow recovery? How do I recover faster after shots? ## Definition Recovery time is the duration from ball contact to ready position for the next shot. It's a critical indicator of movement efficiency and court coverage ability. Slow recovery means you're vulnerable to opponent attacks. ## Why It Matters ### Match Performance - Fast recovery = better court positioning - Good positioning = easier next shot - Consistent recovery = sustained performance through long rallies ### Benchmark Times - **Elite players**: 0.8-1.2 seconds - **Advanced players**: 1.2-1.5 seconds - **Intermediate**: 1.5-2.0 seconds - **>2.0 seconds**: Vulnerable to opponent's attack ## Components of Recovery ### 1. Deceleration After stroke, you must slow down momentum before changing direction. **Technique**: - Outside leg absorbs force - Controlled deceleration (not abrupt) - Maintain balance throughout ### 2. Direction Change Transitioning from stroke direction to recovery direction. **Technique**: - Push off with outside leg - Use small adjustment steps - Keep center of mass low ### 3. Return Movement Moving back to tactical position (usually center or anticipated next shot location). **Technique**: - Efficient path (not circular) - Maintain ready position while moving - Eyes on opponent ### 4. Split Step Preparation Final component: ready to explode in any direction. **Timing**: - Execute split step as opponent contacts ball - Feet shoulder-width apart - Weight on balls of feet ## What Slows Recovery? ### Technique Issues - **Over-hitting**: Excess power creates momentum that's hard to stop - **Poor footwork**: Big steps instead of small adjustments - **High center of mass**: Standing too upright - **Watching your shot**: Not tracking opponent immediately ### Physical Factors - **Fatigue**: Legs tire, recovery slows - **Poor conditioning**: Lack of lateral speed/agility - **Balance issues**: Unstable base requires extra time to stabilize ### Tactical Errors - **Wrong positioning**: Moving to wrong spot wastes time - **Late decision**: Hesitation adds delay - **Passive mindset**: Not anticipating next shot ## Improving Recovery Time ### Technical Improvements 1. **Push-off technique**: Train explosive lateral push from outside leg 2. **Smaller steps**: Replace big strides with quick adjustment steps 3. **Stay low**: Maintain athletic stance throughout movement 4. **Immediate tracking**: Eyes on opponent instantly after your contact ### Physical Training 1. **Lateral agility drills**: Cone drills, ladder drills 2. **Plyometrics**: Box jumps, lateral bounds for explosive power 3. **Core strengthening**: Stability enables faster direction changes 4. **Endurance**: Conditioning to maintain speed when tired ### Practice Drills - **Side-to-side drill with recovery**: Touch sideline, recover to center, repeat - **Shadow strokes with recovery step**: Execute stroke, recover, split step - **Reaction ball drill**: Random directions force quick recovery ## Fatigue's Impact Recovery time is sensitive to fatigue: - **Fresh**: Optimal recovery speed - **Mild fatigue**: 10-15% slower - **Moderate fatigue**: 20-30% slower

title: Serve Fundamentals
text: # Serve Fundamentals ## Overview The serve is the only stroke you fully control. It's the most important stroke in tennis. ## Key Phases ### 1. Starting Position - Feet shoulder-width apart - Front foot at 45° angle to baseline - Weight balanced, relaxed posture - Racket and ball start together ### 2. Ball Toss - **Height**: 6-12 inches above full extension - **Position**: Slightly in front and to right (for right-hander) - **Consistency**: Same spot every time - **Toss arm**: Straight, smooth lift (not throw) ### 3. Loading Phase - Trophy position (both arms up) - Weight shifts to back foot - Knee bend for leg drive - Racket drops behind back (scratch back position) ### 4. Acceleration - Explosive leg drive upward - Hip rotation forward - Shoulder rotation (racket lag) - Pronation begins - Contact at highest point ### 5. Contact - Arm fully extended - Contact slightly in front - Eyes on ball - Pronation at contact for spin/power ### 6. Follow-Through - Racket continues across body - Land on front foot - Deceleration controlled - Recovery step into court ## Key Metrics ### Shoulder Rotation - **Target**: 90-120° rotation - **Why**: Generates racket head speed - **Common issue**: Limited rotation = slow serve ### Knee Bend - **Target**: 30-45° bend before leg drive - **Why**: Leg power adds 30% of serve speed - **Common issue**: Stiff legs = arm-only serve ### Contact Height - **Target**: As high as comfortable full extension - **Why**: Higher contact = steeper angle into service box - **Common issue**: Low contact = higher net clearance needed = less pace ### Pronation - **Target**: Forearm rotates through contact - **Why**: Adds spin and protects elbow - **Common issue**: No pronation = flat serve only, injury risk ## Serve Types ### Flat Serve - Minimal spin, maximum pace - Contact: Center-back of ball - Use: First serve, ace attempts ### Slice Serve - Sidespin, curves away - Contact: Side of ball (3 o'clock for right-hander) - Use: Wide serve, pull opponent off court ### Kick Serve - Heavy topspin, kicks up - Contact: Bottom-side of ball (7 o'clock) - Use: Second serve, high bounce to backhand ## Common Errors ### 1. Inconsistent Toss - **Symptom**: Ball in different spot each serve - **Result**: Timing and contact inconsistent - **Fix**: Toss practice (without hitting), mark target spot ### 2. No Leg Drive - **Symptom**: Stiff legs, no upward explosion - **Result**: Arm-only serve, less power, injury risk - **Fix**: Emphasis on knee bend and leg drive, medicine ball throws ### 3. Elbow Leading - **Symptom**: Elbow comes through before racket - **Result**: Loss of racket lag and power - **Fix**: Pronation drills, serve from knees ### 4. Poor Balance - **Symptom**: Falling sideways or backward - **Result**: Inconsistent contact, slow recovery - **Fix**: Wider stance, better toss placement, core strengthening ## Biomechanical Sequence (Kinetic Chain) 1. **Legs**: Drive upward (30% of power) 2. **Hips**: Rotate forward (20% of power) 3. **Torso**: Rotation and

Elbow Leading - **Symptom**: Elbow comes through before racket - **Result**: Loss of racket lag and power - **Fix**: Pronation drills, serve from knees ### 4. Poor Balance - **Symptom**: Falling sideways or backward - **Result**: Inconsistent contact, slow recovery - **Fix**: Wider stance, better toss placement, core strengthening ## Biomechanical Sequence (Kinetic Chain) 1. **Legs**: Drive upward (30% of power) 2. **Hips**: Rotate forward (20% of power) 3. **Torso**: Rotation and extension (20% of power) 4. **Shoulder**: Rotation and internal rotation (15% of power) 5. **Arm**: Extension and pronation (15% of power) Breaking the chain anywhere reduces power and increases injury risk. ## Training Priorities ### Beginners - Consistent toss - Contact at full extension - Balanced finish ### Intermediate - Leg drive integration - Pronation development - Second serve reliability ### Advanced - Racket lag and speed - Spin variation mastery - Placement precision ## Serve vs Groundstrokes Key differences: - **Serve**: Overhead motion (shoulder stress) - **Serve**: Vertical leg drive (not lateral) - **Serve**: Pronation critical (not needed in groundstrokes) - **Serve**: Timing completely self-controlled Don't apply backhand/forehand expectations to serve biomechanics. ## Safety Note The serve has highest injury risk due to overhead motion and high forces. Proper technique is essential: - Gradual volume increases - Adequate warm-up - Pronation to protect elbow - Leg drive to reduce arm strain - Recovery time between high-volume sessions If shoulder or elbow pain develops, reduce serve volume and consult a professional.

title: Training Load Guidance: Smart Session Planning
text: # Training Load Guidance: Smart Session Planning ## What Is Training Load Guidance? Training load recommendations help you choose the right training focus, intensity, and volume based on your current state. ## Session Types Explained ### Recovery Session **When**: High fatigue, poor readiness, or post-competition **Focus**: Active recovery, mobility, light movement **Intensity**: Low (50-60% effort) **Duration**: 30-45 minutes **Example**: Light rallies, footwork at walking pace, stretching ### Technique Session **When**: Moderate readiness, specific technical issues identified **Focus**: Stroke refinement, drilling fundamentals **Intensity**: Moderate (60-75% effort) **Duration**: 60-90 minutes **Example**: Shadow swings, fed balls, isolated stroke practice ### Movement Session **When**: Technique solid but movement quality low **Focus**: Footwork, agility, court coverage **Intensity**: Moderate to High (70-85% effort) **Duration**: 60-75 minutes **Example**: Cone drills, defensive patterns, recovery training ### Conditioning Session **When**: Good readiness, building physical base **Focus**: Endurance, strength, explosiveness **Intensity**: High (80-90% effort) **Duration**: 45-60 minutes on-court + gym work **Example**: High-rep drills, interval training, resistance work ### Full Training **When**: Excellent readiness, no major concerns **Focus**: All aspects, match simulation **Intensity**: Variable (70-90% effort) **Duration**: 90-120 minutes **Example**: Technical work + point play + conditioning ### Match Simulation **When**: Peak readiness, competition approaching **Focus**: Competitive scenarios, pressure situations **Intensity**: High to Maximum (85-100% effort) **Duration**: 60-90 minutes **Example**: Practice matches, tiebreakers, pressure points ## Intensity Levels Explained ### Low Intensity - **Effort**: 50-60% - **Heart Rate**: <70% max - **Feel**: Conversational, sustainable indefinitely - **Purpose**: Recovery, technique refinement ### Moderate Intensity - **Effort**: 60-75% - **Heart Rate**: 70-80% max - **Feel**: Steady, can maintain for long periods - **Purpose**: Skill development, aerobic base ### High Intensity - **Effort**: 75-90% - **Heart Rate**: 80-90% max - **Feel**: Challenging, breathing hard - **Purpose**: Match-pace training, anaerobic development ### Maximum Intensity - **Effort**: 90-100% - **Heart Rate**: >90% max - **Feel**: All-out, unsustainable >60 seconds - **Purpose**: Competition, explosive power development ## Decision Logic Coach AI uses this decision tree: ### If Fatigue is High (>75) → **Recovery Session, Low Intensity** - Rest is productive training - Avoid technique work (fatigue prevents quality) - Focus on mobility and restoration ### If Signal Trust is Low (<60%) → **Re-record recommended** - Consider light Technique Session with new recording - Low intensity (don't push on uncertain data) ### If Readiness is Excellent (>80) → **Full Training or Match Simulation** - Opportunity for intense work - High-quality practice produces best results - Consider competition scheduling ### If Readiness is Good (65-79) → **Normal Training** - Mix technique, movement, and play - Moderate to high intensity based on fatigue - Progressive overload ### If Readiness is Fair (50-64) → **Technique or Movement Focus** - Address specific weaknesses - Moderate intensity only - Avoid high-volume or high-intensity work ### If Readiness is Poor (<50) → **Recovery or Light Technique** - Reduce training load - Low intensity only - Investigate causes (overtraining? illness?) ## Focus and Avoid Areas ### Focus Areas Lists specific metrics/skills to work on: - Example: "Hip rotation", "Recovery time", "Balance" - Drill recommendations

Progress tracked session-to-session ### Avoid Areas Lists what to rest or minimize: - Example: "High-volume footwork" (if fatigue high) - Example: "Intensive drilling" (if technique is fatigued) - Prevents overloading weak areas ## Progressive Overload Training should follow a cycle: 1. **Stimulus**: Challenging session (technique, movement, or conditioning) 2. **Fatigue**: Temporary performance dip, readiness decreases 3. **Recovery**: Lighter sessions, readiness rebounds 4. **Adaptation**: Performance improves above previous baseline Coach AI helps you navigate this cycle: - Hard days when readiness is high - Easy days when fatigue appears - Recovery before readiness drops too low ## Weekly Training Structure (Example) ### High Readiness Week - Mon: Full Training (High intensity) - Tue: Technique Session (Moderate) - Wed: Match Simulation (High) - Thu: Movement Session (Moderate) - Fri: Recovery (Low) - Sat: Competition or Match Sim - Sun: Off ### Moderate Readiness Week - Mon: Technique Session (Moderate) - Tue: Movement Session (Moderate) - Wed: Recovery (Low) - Thu: Technique Session (Moderate) - Fri: Light Match Play (Moderate) - Sat: Off or Recovery - Sun: Off ### Low Readiness Week (Recovery Week) - Mon: Recovery (Low) - Tue: Off - Wed: Light Technique (Low) - Thu: Recovery (Low) - Fri: Off - Sat: Light Match Play (Low-Moderate) - Sun: Off ## Confidence Score Training load recommendations include confidence: - **High (>80%)**: All inputs reliable, follow recommendation - **Medium (60-80%)**: Some uncertainty, use judgment - **Low (<60%)**: Limited data, rely more on feel Always combine data with self-awareness. ## When to Override Recommendations ### Trust Your Body - If you feel great but readiness is fair → can train harder - If you feel terrible but readiness is good → rest ### Life Context - High stress, poor sleep → reduce intensity regardless of readiness - Important competition soon → adjust training regardless of readiness ### Injury or Illness - Always trumps readiness scores - Rest and recover first ## Integration with Progress Tracking Training load adapts to your trends: - **Improving trend**: Gradually increase load - **Stable trend**: Maintain current approach or add stimulus - **Declining trend**: Reduce load, emphasize recovery This prevents overtraining and optimizes adaptation. ## Key Principles 1. **Hard days hard, easy days easy**: Avoid "moderate everything" 2. **Recovery is training**: Adaptation happens during rest 3. **Quality over quantity**: Better to do less with excellence 4. **Listen to your body**: Data informs, you decide
